title: When a Complete Baller Wont Talk About It
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Anchored in the story of an anonymous Augusta National member who serves as a non-competitive 'Marker' at the Masters — playing in the tournament without being announced, interviewed, or shown on camera — this essay draws a leadership parallel about knowing when to step out of the spotlight. It notes that the CEO who played the Marker role, praised by pro golfer Tom Kim as a 'complete baller,' had to suppress the instinct most executives have to be visible and vocal. The piece argues that a leader unwilling or unable to occasionally play a supporting, uncredited role inside their own organization is not much of a leader, and that toggling between visibility and quiet service takes deliberate practice.
points: Uses the Masters' anonymous 'Marker' tradition as a metaphor for a leader's willingness to take an uncredited supporting role.
Argues that CEOs who can't suppress the impulse to be visible and vocal in every setting are limited as leaders.
Frames the capacity to alternate between outspoken leadership and quiet, uncredited service as a deliberately practiced skill, not an innate trait.
Ties the anecdote to a specific real person — Augusta member Michael McDermott — grounding the metaphor in a verifiable news event.
Suggests humility and confidence together, not humility alone, are what make the Marker role possible for a leader.
quotes: Each year, this mysterious man who plays Augusta National on the weekends as a member gets to play in the tournament without ever qualifying for the field. The Club doesn’t talk about him, and the broadcast crews are instructed not to show him on camera.
How did this stand-in do? Tom Kim, in his post-tournament press conference, called him a “complete baller,” which is another way of saying this guy can really play.

A CEO who can’t play the role of a Marker inside their own organization is probably not much of a Chief Executive. To act nothing more than a guy or gal standing in on some project or task is exactly what makes them worth following.
The best leaders act as a Marker on purpose at times to exercise this muscle and to show others that they are not above playing any role the organization needs.
The flexibility to sometimes be the outspoken leader and sometimes be the Marker doesn’t come naturally for anyone. It takes humility, confidence, and a knowledge of what leadership is all about.
